title: Routing contracts and SLA boundaries for tenant routing
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note to define a minimal, implementable set of routing contracts (what the control plane guarantees and what the data plane is allowed to do) and the associated SLA / isolation boundaries we will expose to product teams for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment modes. Aim is to be operationally tight enough to avoid ambiguous ownership while allowing the serving runtime and infra to make efficient routing decisions.

High level goals:
- Make per-tenant routing guarantees explicit: latency SLOs, egress locality, allowed failover tiers (same-region, cross-region, fallback model variants).
- Define ingress/egress boundaries (who owns NAT, who performs TLS termination, control-plane coordination).
- Ensure that cost-saving behaviors (batching, caching rerouting) have predictable effects on tenant isolation and SLA.
- Produce a small matrix teams can use when onboarding new tenants or approving Dedicated/Private contracts.

Key terms (informal definitions):
- Routing contract: a terse statement of what routing behaviors the platform can perform for a tenant (e.g., cross-region spill allowed, automatic model fallback allowed).
- Isolation boundary: network and multi-tenancy limits (e.g., shared runtime vs dedicated node pool, VPC peering).
- Control plane lease: the set of metadata and active routing policies the control plane can mutate for a tenant during runtime.
- Tenant egress model: where tenant egress IPs are NATed and what is reachable from the compute plane.

Summary of guarantees per deployment mode (first pass):
1) Hosted (multi-tenant, Redwood-managed):
   - Routing contract: platform may route to any compatible model variant within the same region; cross-region routing allowed for failover only (incurs higher-latency SLO).
   - Isolation boundaries: logical tenant isolation via model-level k/v cache and per-tenant quotas. No guaranteed private network, egress originates from shared NAT IP ranges (documented IP ranges).
   - Control plane: full control; may perform model-variant fallbacks, autoscaling, and batching optimizations without tenant approval; will notify via audit events for policy changes affecting SLA tier.
   - SLA: published regional P95 latency and error-rate targets for each SKU; best-effort routing to improve cost (e.g., batching) but cost-driven batching will not violate published latency SLO for paid tiers.
   - Failure semantics: on capacity shortage platform can fallback to smaller models or cross-region endpoints; tenants on paid tiers can opt into isolation guarantees (see Dedicated).

2) Dedicated (reserved GPU pools for a customer):
   - Routing contract: tenant routing stays inside the customer’s dedicated pool where possible. The platform may spill to Redwood-managed warm standby in the same region if explicit spill policy enabled.
   - Isolation boundaries: dedicated node pools, dedicated model pinning; network egress still exits through Redwood NAT unless customer requests VPC egress (Private add-on).
   - Control plane: customer-level policy controls rollout windows and can opt out of automated cross-tenant batching; platform retains control over infra-level failover within the dedicated pool.
   - SLA: stronger latency and throughput guarantees tied to reserved capacity. Dedicated SLA includes bounds on autoscaling times and max spill thresholds before throttling.
   - Failure semantics: if the dedicated pool is saturated, either queue/ingest throttle or controlled spill to a pre-agreed fallback target (explicit contract).

3) Private (VPC / on-prem):
   - Routing contract: routing is restricted to customer-managed networking. Platform control-plane actions that require routing changes must be explicitly permitted in the customer’s onboarding agreement.
   - Isolation boundaries: full network isolation (VPC peering, private control-plane VPN or on-prem control); egress follows customer-managed NAT. No shared-data plane mixing.
   - Control plane: control plane runs in private mode (either customer-hosted control plane or a private tenant overlay). Remote actions (model updates, metrics telemetry) require explicit connectors and tenant consent for data egress.
   - SLA: SLAs can be negotiated but are based on the customer’s infra characteristics. Redwood guarantees best-effort infra ops; more prescriptive SLAs require host-level support and runbook attachments.
   - Failure semantics: platform cannot unilaterally route tenant compute outside the private boundary; any cross-region work requires explicit network peering or customer-approved fallback policies.

Routing primitives we expose (API/contract level):
- prefer_region: list of preferred regions (ordered). No implicit region amplification.
- allow_cross_region_failover: boolean (default false for Private; true for Hosted with constraints; configurable for Dedicated).
- fallback_models: ordered list of model identifiers to use when primary is unavailable or throttled.
- egress_profile: one of [shared_nat, dedicated_nat, customer_managed_vpc].

Operational notes and gotchas (from past incidents):
- Silent cross-region fallbacks increased P50 for a small percentage of traffic when batching thresholds waited for cross-region nodes to be ready. Mitigation: add region-aware batching cutoff and a per-request region-affinity hint.
- Caching semantics differ by tenancy: shared cache eviction policy can cause regenerative compute spikes. For Dedicated, provide an optional per-tenant cache partition to reduce noisy neighbor eviction.
- TLS termination ownership must be clear: Hosted terminates at edge (platform), Private usually requires tenant to terminate or validate certificate provisioning via KMS/HSM integration.

Decision matrix (quick):
- If tenant needs static egress IPs + guaranteed compute locality -> Private with customer_managed_vpc + explicit allow_cross_region_failover=false.
- If tenant needs predictable throughput and moderate isolation but still wants Redwood operational simplicity -> Dedicated with dedicated_nat and explicit spill policy.
- If tenant prioritizes time-to-value and accepts shared infrastructure -> Hosted (default), with subscription-based SLA tiers controlling batching aggressiveness.

Example onboarding checklist items (to be appended to customer SOP):
- Confirm egress_profile and update firewall allowlist with documented IP ranges (Hosted) or validate VPC peering instructions (Private).
- Choose fallback_models and confirm contract on automatic fallbacks and cost implications.
- Decide on telemetry/metrics reporting level and whether control plane may trigger automated model rollbacks.
- For Dedicated: define max_spill_target and throttle behavior in the contract.

Open questions / items to resolve:
- How granular should the region-affinity hint be? per-request header vs per-route config? (action: product + runtime to prototype both by Q1 2025)
- Should we allow per-tenant overrides of batching window when under a paid SLA? (action: cost modeling required; PLAT-4821 assigned)
- Telemetry throttling for Private: how do we ensure platform health signals without leaking tenant data? (action: security to propose sanitized telemetry contract)

Notes and links:
- Incident learnings: refer to PLAT-3810 (cross-region spill incident) and postmortem notes on Confluence in the linked artifact.
- Dev work: see infra PR #2173 for early region-aware batch cutoff prototype.
- Slack thread: #platform-routing for design discussion and rapid feedback.

Next steps (short):
- Iterate this doc into a short JSON schema for routing contracts (owner: Leah) so product can render onboarding UI.
- Run tabletop with SRE and Solutions Eng to validate worst-case failure semantics for Dedicated spill policy (owner: Diego).
- Draft minimal external-facing excerpt for sales and customer onboarding docs (owner: Rohit).
